claims.text: A combined electromagnetic-levitation, synchrotron X-ray, and high-speed-calorimetry approach can determine melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, melting volume change, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the high-entropy-alloy family.
Suitable starting materials are as-cast HEA ingots with minimal microstructural heterogeneity.
The starting ingots are free of prior container-induced contaminants.
HEA samples can be electromagnetically levitated under high vacuum or inert atmosphere while high-speed calorimetry and synchrotron X-ray measurements are performed simultaneously.
Heating rates of 100–200 K/s are suitable for measurements through HEA melting transitions.
The relevant melting-temperature range is approximately 1200–2000 K.
High vacuum or inert atmosphere minimizes oxidation and contamination during these measurements.
Containerless processing eliminates container-induced heterogeneous nucleation and contamination.
The proposed X-ray measurements can capture atomic-scale density fluctuations in the liquid in real time.
Containerless processing prevents extrinsic nucleation sites and heat loss.
Synchronizing calorimetry with X-ray radiography provides complementary thermal and structural information.
The combined measurements improve detection of phase transitions, latent-heat absorption, and melting-associated volume changes.
The proposed technique will measure melting temperatures to within ±5 K.
The proposed technique will measure latent heat with uncertainty around ±10 J/g.
Fusion entropy will be measured with relative errors similar to those of the latent-heat measurement.
Melting-associated volume change will be evaluated with 0.1–0.5% error.
Conventional container-based DSC and high-temperature density measurements are often compromised by contamination and non-uniform heating.
The approach is most effective for HEAs melting above approximately 1200 K that can be electromagnetically levitated.
Applicability may be limited for very low-melting or highly reactive alloy systems.
Fusion entropy can be derived from measured latent heat and melting temperature.

contradictions.description: The predicted melting-temperature accuracy is ±5 K, whereas falsification permits deviations as large as ±5%, which is roughly ±60–100 K over the stated 1200–2000 K range. The validation threshold is therefore much weaker than the claimed performance.

The X-ray modality is described inconsistently as diffraction, imaging, and radiography. Volume change is specifically assigned to diffraction in the validation plan, while density monitoring is assigned to imaging or radiography elsewhere.
